title: Are AI Tutors Really Teaching Students — or Just Teaching the Test?
author: The Digital Delusion
summary: In the second of a two-part series on transfer of learning, the author uses the rise and fall of the billion-dollar brain training industry as the central case study for understanding why AI tutoring platforms may be repeating the same structural error. The article distinguishes near transfer (applying learning to closely similar contexts) from far transfer (applying learning across substantially different contexts), drawing on a 2016 meta-analysis of 87 working-memory training studies that found working memory tasks improve sharply in near-transfer conditions but produce no statistically significant gains in far-transfer measures—a finding that explains precisely why Lumosity-style programs collapsed after initial enthusiasm. The author applies this framework to AI tutors, arguing that students who become proficient within a tutoring environment may struggle to carry that learning into novel situations, and that the closer an assessment resembles the learning environment, the more likely it is to overestimate what students have actually learned. The piece examines PISA, TIMSS, and NAEP data showing that greater reliance on digital tutoring correlates with lower performance on assessments removed from the tutoring environment. The central argument is that the true test of any educational technology is not what students can do with the tutor but what they can still do without it—a criterion the current generation of AI tutoring platforms has yet to satisfy—and that rising standardized test scores may simply reflect assessments that have become more similar to the tutoring environment, not deeper learning.
points: Near transfer (applying learning to similar contexts) and far transfer (applying learning across dissimilar contexts) operate on fundamentally different mechanisms—and a 2016 meta-analysis of 87 working-memory training studies found near-transfer gains but zero statistically significant far-transfer improvement, which explains why the billion-dollar brain training industry collapsed.

PISA (2012, 2015, 2018), TIMSS (2019, 2023), and NAEP (2017, 2019, 2022, 2024) all show the same pattern: greater reliance on digital tutoring activities correlates with lower performance on assessments removed from the tutoring environment, consistent with the near-transfer-only hypothesis.

Effective curricula deliberately vary context, medium, mode, and instructional approach so students internalize the underlying conceptual structure rather than the surface features of a particular learning environment—a design principle that most AI tutoring platforms implicitly violate by optimizing for performance within a single interface.

The closer an assessment resembles the learning environment, the more likely it is to overestimate what students have actually learned; reported AI-tutor effectiveness figures should therefore be read with scrutiny of how and where the outcome was measured.

The redesign of the SAT to an adaptive digital format illustrates how rising test scores attributed to digital tutors may simply reflect the fact that the assessment itself has become more similar to the tutoring environment—not that deeper or more transferable learning occurred.
quotes: Near transfer occurs when learning is applied to a new situation that closely resembles the one in which it was acquired. The underlying structure, environment, and goals are the largely same - only minor details change.

Far transfer occurs when learning is successfully applied to a situation that differs substantially from the original learning context. While the underlying principles remain consistent, the structure, environment, and goals may all have changed.

As any educator can attest, transfer - even relatively near transfer - is one of the greatest challenges in learning. It is remarkably common for students to perform well in one setting yet struggle to apply that same knowledge in another.

This is precisely why (as discussed in our previous post) effective curricula deliberately vary the way students encounter new ideas. Rather than practicing one type of problem repeatedly in one context, students explore the same underlying concept through different modes (writing, speaking, acting), different media (textbooks, whiteboards, flashcards), different environments (the classroom, the laboratory, field trips), and different instructional approaches (explicit instruction, hands-on demonstrations, group discussions).
From Pressey’s teaching machine to brain training to AI tutors, the promise has remained the same: master the program, and that mastery will generalize to the wider world.

The major point here isn’t that students can’t learn from digital tutors – they clearly can. It’s that the learning they produce is often more contextualized, less durable, and less transferable than knowledge developed through more traditional pedagogies. Equally important, where and how we measure learning matters enormously: the closer an assessment resembles the learning environment, the more likely it is to overestimate what students have actually learned.
Put simply, the effectiveness of any digital tutor cannot be separated from the transfer demands of the assessment used to evaluate it.
Ultimately, the true test of learning is not what students can do with the tutor - but what they can still do without it.
